chapter_title: Control Plane and Management Plane Protection
chapter_summary:
Securing the network infrastructure isn't just about protecting user data; it's equally, if not more, about protecting the network devices themselves. A compromised router or switch can bring down an entire network, regardless of how secure the data plane is. This is where Control Plane Policing (CoPP) and Management Plane Protection (MPP) become indispensable. The **control plane** of a network device is responsible for handling traffic destined to or generated by the device itself, such as routing protocol updates (OSPF, EIGRP, BGP), ARP requests, ICMP messages, AAA traffic, and management protocols (SSH, SNMP). Attacks targeting the control plane, like denial-of-service (DoS) attacks, can overwhelm the device's CPU, leading to instability, routing blackholes, or complete device unresponsiveness. CoPP is designed to mitigate these threats by rate-limiting or dropping malicious traffic before it can impact the control plane's stability.

**Control Plane Policing (CoPP)** uses the Modular QoS CLI (MQC) framework to classify and apply policies to traffic destined for the control plane. The core idea is to identify legitimate control plane traffic, prioritize it, and then rate-limit or drop any excess or unauthorized traffic. This prevents a single type of attack, like a flood of malformed packets or excessive routing updates, from consuming all CPU resources. Implementing CoPP involves three main steps:
1.  **Class-maps:** Define traffic classes based on various criteria, such as protocol (e.g., OSPF, BGP, SSH), port numbers, or ACLs. You'll typically create classes for legitimate routing protocols, management traffic, and a default class for all other control plane traffic.
2.  **Policy-map:** Define actions for each class, such as `police` (rate-limit) or `drop`. For critical protocols, you might set a specific committed information rate (CIR) and a burst size. For unknown or suspicious traffic, you might drop it or police it to a very low rate.
3.  **Service-policy:** Apply the policy-map to the control plane using the `control-plane` interface configuration mode.

A common mistake in CoPP configuration is being too aggressive with policing rates for legitimate traffic, which can inadvertently disrupt routing protocols or management access. It's crucial to understand the normal traffic patterns of your control plane and set appropriate policing rates. For instance, OSPF hellos are frequent but small; BGP updates can be large during convergence. You need to account for these variations. Always start with a conservative approach and monitor the `show policy-map control-plane` output to identify dropped packets and adjust rates as needed. A typical CoPP strategy involves creating separate classes for established TCP connections (e.g., SSH, BGP), routing protocols, ICMP, and then a catch-all class with a very low police rate or even a drop action for anything else.

```cli
! Example CoPP Configuration Snippet
ip access-list extended COPP_SSH
 permit tcp any any eq 22
ip access-list extended COPP_OSPF
 permit ospf any any
!
class-map match-any CM_SSH
 match access-group name COPP_SSH
class-map match-any CM_OSPF
 match access-group name COPP_OSPF
class-map CM_DEFAULT_CP
 match default-class
!
policy-map PM_CONTROL_PLANE
 class CM_SSH
  police cir 8000 bc 8000 conform-action transmit exceed-action drop
 class CM_OSPF
  police cir 16000 bc 16000 conform-action transmit exceed-action drop
 class CM_DEFAULT_CP
  police cir 4000 bc 4000 conform-action drop exceed-action drop
!
control-plane
 service-policy input PM_CONTROL_PLANE
```

**Management Plane Protection (MPP)** is a simpler, yet equally vital, feature that restricts which interfaces can be used for management access (e.g., Telnet, SSH, SNMP, HTTP/HTTPS) to the device. By default, management access is typically allowed on all interfaces. MPP allows you to explicitly define a set of interfaces as "management interfaces," meaning only traffic received on these interfaces can access the device's management services. This prevents an attacker from trying to manage the device through a data-plane interface that might be less secure or more exposed. For example, you might restrict management access only to a dedicated out-of-band management interface or a specific in-band VLAN interface.

MPP configuration is straightforward:
```cli
! Example MPP Configuration Snippet
control-plane host
 management-interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0 allow ssh snmp
 management-interface Vlan10 allow ssh http
```
In this example, only SSH and SNMP traffic arriving on Gi0/0/0, and SSH and HTTP traffic arriving on Vlan10, will be processed by the control plane for management purposes. Any management traffic on other interfaces will be dropped. A common safety note for both CoPP and MPP is to avoid locking yourself out of the device. Always test configurations in a lab, and if implementing remotely, ensure you have an out-of-band management channel or a local console connection as a fallback. Overly restrictive CoPP policies can cause routing adjacencies to drop or prevent legitimate management access. Overly restrictive MPP can prevent access from necessary monitoring tools or authorized administrators. Careful planning and monitoring are essential for both. These features, when correctly implemented, significantly harden your network devices against direct attacks, contributing to overall network stability and security.

screens.subtitle: Why device-focused defenses like CoPP and MPP are essential for network stability

narration.text: In this lesson we focus on defending the parts of a router that actually make decisions and accept administrative requests. The control plane handles traffic destined to the device itself — routing protocol updates, ARP, ICMP, AAA, and management protocols — and a flood or malicious packets here can consume C P U and destabilize the entire network. Control Plane Policing, or CoPP, uses the Modular QoS CLI to classify control-plane traffic and apply rate limits so that legitimate control protocols continue functioning while abusive or unexpected flows are throttled or dropped. Management Plane Protection, or MPP, complements CoPP by limiting which interfaces and protocols are allowed to reach device management services such as SSH, SNMP, and HTTP. Together they reduce attack surface and preserve reachability. Across the lesson we will study MQC components, safe policing values, verification commands, and a practical lab applying CoPP and MPP to a core router. You will learn concrete configuration snippets, how to interpret show outputs, and common errors that can lock out admins. By the end, you’ll understand how to protect the device without disrupting legitimate operations and what safety checks to use before committing changes.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Protect the device first: use CoPP to rate-limit control-plane traffic and MPP to restrict which interfaces can manage the device, then monitor and tune to avoid accidental service disruption.

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain why CoPP and MPP are necessary, and configure them safely on an IOS XE router. First, you will describe the control plane’s responsibilities and identify the traffic that must reach it, such as routing updates, AAA, and management protocols. Second, you will build and apply CoPP using MQC components: class-map to identify traffic, policy-map to set policing or drop actions, and service-policy to attach the policy to the control plane. Third, you will configure Management Plane Protection to restrict which interfaces can deliver management protocols like SSH and SNMP, reducing the attack surface. Fourth, you will analyze the operational impact of policing and MPP settings, read show-policy outputs, and tune rates to avoid disrupting legitimate protocols. Each objective pairs a practical skill with an operational safety check so you can harden devices without accidentally locking out administrators.

screens.title: What the Control Plane Does and Why It Matters
screens.subtitle: Define control plane traffic and identify critical flows that must be protected

narration.text: The control plane is the set of processes and messages a device uses to learn topology and manage itself. It includes routing protocol exchanges such as OSPF, BGP, or EIGRP updates; ARP requests and replies needed for next-hop resolution; ICMP messages used for diagnostics; AAA traffic for authentication; and management protocols like SSH, SNMP, and HTTP. Because the control plane consumes C P U and memory resources directly on the device, attackers who flood it with malicious or unexpected packets can induce C P U exhaustion, causing routing instability or full device unresponsiveness. A good defense starts with classification: identify which packets are legitimate control-plane traffic and which are not. For example, OSPF hellos are small and frequent, so policing must allow steady small bursts; BGP updates may be large during convergence and require a higher or adaptive allowance. A common misconception is thinking all control-plane traffic is low-volume and safe to police aggressively. In reality, legitimate control messages can be bursty during topology changes. The practical takeaway is to map all essential control flows, prioritize them in CoPP, and reserve a cautious default for any unknown traffic to avoid breaking routing or management functions. How would you map your network’s routing and management flows before applying any policy?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Control plane traffic is any packet destined to or generated by the device; protect it by identifying legitimate flows and allowing them sufficient headroom.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.3 › What the Control Plane Does
Definition

Control plane responsibilities

The control plane handles routing, ARP, ICMP, AAA, and management traffic destined to the device itself. Because these consume CPU, they must be protected from floods and malicious packets.

Common control-plane flows
  • Routing protocol exchanges (OSPF, BGP): topology updates and hellos.
  • AAA and management protocols (SSH, SNMP): authentication and monitoring.
  • ICMP and ARP: diagnostics and neighbor resolution.
Misconception
Assuming control-plane traffic is always low volume. During convergence, legitimate traffic can spike and must be allowed sufficient rate to keep adjacencies alive.
Analogy & Example

Think of the control plane as a switchboard operator inside the device. If the operator is overwhelmed, calls fail even if the external wires are intact. For example, if a router under attack cannot process OSPF LSAs, routing adjacencies drop and packets are blackholed.

Key takeaway
Identify critical control-plane traffic before applying policies and reserve headroom for bursts during convergence.
Check your understanding
Which protocol would you raise the policing allowance for during topology changes: OSPF or SSH? Consider message frequency and burst behavior.

screens.title: CoPP with MQC: Class‑map → Policy‑map → Service‑policy
screens.subtitle: The three-step Modular QoS CLI pattern for controlling the control plane

narration.text: Control Plane Policing uses the Modular QoS CLI pattern: first classify traffic with class-maps, then define actions in a policy-map, and finally attach the policy-map to the control plane using a service-policy. Class-maps let you match traffic using ACLs, protocol matches, or default-class for everything else. In practice you create classes for critical flows such as SSH and routing protocols, and a default class to catch unknown control-plane packets. The policy-map binds policing behavior to each class. For critical control traffic you commonly set a committed information rate and a burst size, allowing legitimate packets while policing excess. For unknown or suspicious traffic you choose a very low police rate or drop completely. Finally use control-plane service-policy input to enforce the rules. A common mistake is to forget the service-policy step or to apply it to the wrong direction. Always verify with show policy-map control-plane and inspect packet and drop counters. Start with conservative policing values in a lab, monitor counters, and then adjust. The essential claim is simple: MQC separates identification, action, and attachment so you can reason about which flows are protected and how enforcement will behave under load. What class would you create first on a new router, and why?

keyIdea.title: Three-step MQC
keyIdea.text: Classify with class-map, enforce with policy-map, apply with service-policy to the control plane; verify and iterate using show outputs.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.3 › CoPP MQC Pattern
Process

Class-map → Policy-map → Service-policy

This pattern separates identification, enforcement, and application, which makes CoPP predictable and auditable.

Step 1 — Classify
Use ACLs and protocol matches to create classes like CM_SSH, CM_OSPF, and a default class for all other control-plane traffic.
Step 2 — Define actions
In a policy-map, set police rates, burst sizes, and drop behaviors per class. Reserve higher rates for routing protocols when needed.
Step 3 — Attach
Use control-plane service-policy input to apply the policy to traffic destined to the device.
Code example
ip access-list extended COPP_SSH
 permit tcp any any eq 22
ip access-list extended COPP_OSPF
 permit ospf any any
!
class-map match-any CM_SSH
 match access-group name COPP_SSH
class-map match-any CM_OSPF
 match access-group name COPP_OSPF
class-map CM_DEFAULT_CP
 match default-class
!
policy-map PM_CONTROL_PLANE
 class CM_SSH
  police cir 8000 bc 8000 conform-action transmit exceed-action drop
 class CM_OSPF
  police cir 16000 bc 16000 conform-action transmit exceed-action drop
 class CM_DEFAULT_CP
  police cir 4000 bc 4000 conform-action drop exceed-action drop
!
control-plane
 service-policy input PM_CONTROL_PLANE
Example
SSH is policed to 8 kbps so interactive sessions remain usable while preventing SSH flood abuse.
Common-mistake
Applying aggressive policing to routing classes that then drop LSAs and break adjacencies.

screens.title: Class‑maps and ACLs: Practical Classification
screens.subtitle: Create targeted ACLs and class-maps to match SSH, OSPF, and a default control-plane class

narration.text: Accurate classification is the foundation of CoPP. You begin by writing ACLs that match the specific management and routing traffic you trust. For SSH, a simple extended ACL permitting TCP eq 22 suffices; for OSPF, permit ospf any any captures OSPF packets. Then create class-maps that reference those ACL names. Use match-any when a class should match multiple ACLs or protocols. Always include a class that matches default-class so you can handle everything else explicitly. A practical example from our source shows naming conventions like COPP_SSH and CM_SSH. Naming consistently helps operations teams audit and understand policies later. When you test, validate the ACLs with packet captures or by temporarily permitting the same traffic with a loose access-list to observe behavior. A common misconception is to match too broadly — for instance permitting TCP any any eq 22 without restricting source ranges when management should be limited to trusted admin subnets. The concrete step: create targeted ACLs, map them into named class-maps, and leave a conservative default class for unknown control-plane traffic. Which ACL would you tighten first in a mixed in-band and out-of-band environment?

keyIdea.title: Classification principle
keyIdea.text: Write precise ACLs for management and routing flows, use named class-maps to reference them, and include a default-class to catch unexpected control-plane traffic.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.3 › Class-maps & ACLs
How to

Create ACLs for control-plane traffic

Target management and routing flows with precise ACL entries. Consider source restrictions for SSH to limit admin subnets.

ip access-list extended COPP_SSH
 permit tcp any any eq 22
ip access-list extended COPP_OSPF
 permit ospf any any
Class-maps
Reference ACLs inside class-maps so the policy-map can apply policing per named class.
class-map match-any CM_SSH
 match access-group name COPP_SSH
class-map match-any CM_OSPF
 match access-group name COPP_OSPF
class-map CM_DEFAULT_CP
 match default-class
Practical notes
  • Use descriptive names to make audits easier.
  • Prefer match access-group name so you can reuse ACLs across policies.
  • Keep a default-class to ensure unknown traffic is controlled.
Misconfiguration risk
A broad ACL that permits any source for SSH increases attack surface. Scope ACLs to admin IP ranges when possible.
Quick example
If admins use an out-of-band network, restrict COPP_SSH to that source subnet to reduce risk from the data plane.

screens.title: Policing Parameters — CIR, Burst, and Actions
screens.subtitle: How police statements control rate, bursts, and behavior under exceed conditions

narration.text: When you set policing behavior in a policy-map you choose a committed information rate and a burst size that together determine how much traffic is allowed before packets are dropped or marked. The committed information rate, or CIR, is a steady-state allowance measured in bits per second. The burst (BC) allows short-term spikes above CIR so legitimate transient bursts — like a BGP update or a cluster of OSPF LSAs during convergence — can pass. The policy snippet in the chapter sets SSH to 8 kilobits and OSPF to 16 kilobits with corresponding burst values. The action on exceed can be a drop or a lower-priority handling; in CoPP you commonly use drop to prevent excess flows from consuming C P U. A frequent operational error is choosing CIR and BC too low, which causes legitimate control-plane messages to be dropped and leads to adjacency failures or missed management sessions. The test-and-tune approach is recommended: apply conservative values, monitor show policy-map control-plane for packet and drop counters, then raise values where you see drops for legitimate traffic. Always document why a class has its particular CIR so future engineers can understand the operational tradeoffs. Which traffic would you allow a larger burst for, and why?

keyIdea.title: Policing basics
keyIdea.text: CIR limits steady rate; burst allows short spikes. Set exceed actions deliberately and tune based on observed drops to avoid harming legitimate control protocols.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.3 › Policing Parameters
Parameter details

CIR and burst explained

CIR is the steady allowance. Burst (BC) permits short spikes. Exceed-action determines whether excess packets are dropped.

Example from config
SSH policed to 8000 bps with bc 8000; OSPF policed to 16000 bps with bc 16000.
Operational risk
Setting CIR or BC too low can drop LSAs or update messages, breaking routing adjacencies during convergence.
Visual comparison
Steady-state (CIR)
Defines the long-term permitted rate in bits per second.
Burst (BC)
Allows short bursts above CIR so legitimate transient traffic isn’t dropped.
Practical tip
Monitor counters after deployment and increase CIR or BC for classes showing legitimate drops during spikes.

screens.title: Apply and Verify CoPP — service-policy and show output
screens.subtitle: Attach PM to control plane and interpret show policy-map control-plane output

narration.text: After you define class-maps and a policy-map, the final step is to attach the policy to the control plane using control-plane service-policy input. Once applied, verification is crucial: use show policy-map control-plane to inspect class counters, packet counts, and drops. The output shows how many packets matched each class and how many were policed or dropped. This is the primary operational feedback loop that tells you whether policing values are too strict. When you see drops for a critical class, investigate whether the traffic was legitimate and adjust CIR or BC accordingly. Common noise to watch for includes transient drops during legitimate network convergence or measurement artifacts from test traffic. Another verification technique is staged deployment: apply CoPP in monitor mode or with conservative rates in a maintenance window and correlate show outputs with management system logs. Remember to document changes and include rollback steps. The core claim: attaching a policy is quick, but careful verification and iterative tuning are what keep routing and management working under load. After viewing counters, what one metric would you check first to decide whether to increase a class’s CIR?

keyIdea.title: Verify & iterate
keyIdea.text: Use show policy-map control-plane to read packet and drop counters, then adjust policing values for classes showing legitimate drops.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.3 › Apply & Verify CoPP
Attachment

Apply the policy to the control-plane

Use control-plane service-policy input and then use show policy-map control-plane for verification.

control-plane
 service-policy input PM_CONTROL_PLANE
What to inspect
  • Matched packets per class
  • Policed or dropped packet counts
  • Whether drops align with expected test events or real spikes
Example output (abstracted)
Policy Map PM_CONTROL_PLANE
 Class CM_SSH
  packets: 1200, drops: 2
 Class CM_OSPF
  packets: 4500, drops: 0
 Class CM_DEFAULT_CP
  packets: 7000, drops: 120
Interpretation
Non-zero drops in the default class suggest unknown control-plane traffic is being limited; evaluate whether those packets are malicious or legitimate before changing policies.

screens.title: Management Plane Protection (MPP)
screens.subtitle: Restrict which interfaces and protocols can access the device's management services

narration.text: Management Plane Protection restricts which interfaces the device accepts management traffic from. By default many devices will process management protocols arriving on any interface; MPP flips this by explicitly permitting only listed interfaces and protocols. The configuration uses control-plane host with management-interface statements that name an interface and allowed protocols, for example allowing SSH and SNMP on a dedicated GigabitEthernet interface or permitting SSH and HTTP on a specific VLAN interface. The practical benefit is reducing the device attack surface: management requests arriving on untrusted data plane interfaces are dropped before they reach the control plane. A critical safety rule is to avoid locking yourself out. Always verify that you have console or out-of-band access before applying restrictive MPP statements. The design principle is simple: allow management only where expected. A common error is assuming MPP blocks routing protocols; it does not — MPP controls management protocols, while CoPP handles routing and other control-plane messages. After you define management-interface statements, test access from both allowed and disallowed interfaces to confirm behavior. Management Plane Protection (MPP) means mpp permits management protocols only on explicitly configured interfaces, shrinking attack surface while requiring careful planning to avoid lockout.. In practical terms, restrict which interfaces and protocols can access the device's management services. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: MPP summary
keyIdea.text: MPP permits management protocols only on explicitly configured interfaces, shrinking attack surface while requiring careful planning to avoid lockout.

content.html:
Module 08 › Chapter 8.3 › Management Plane Protection
Definition

What MPP enforces

MPP defines which interfaces may deliver management protocols to the control plane, preventing management traffic on unintended interfaces.

control-plane host
 management-interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0 allow ssh snmp
 management-interface Vlan10 allow ssh http
Safety note
Ensure console or out-of-band access is available before tightening MPP to avoid administrative lockout.
Quick checklist
  • List management protocols required by operations.
  • Identify trusted management interfaces and VLANs.
  • Apply management-interface allow entries for each.
  • Test access and keep a rollback path.
Example
Only allow SSH and SNMP on a dedicated out-of-band GigabitEthernet port to reduce exposure from in-band data traffic.

screens.title: Lab: Implementing CoPP and MPP on R1 (Starter Commands)
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step starter configuration for the hands-on scenario

narration.text: In the hands-on activity you will secure router R1 by implementing CoPP for SSH and OSPF and applying MPP to restrict management to GigabitEthernet0/0/0. Begin in global configuration mode. Create two extended ACLs named COPP_SSH and COPP_OSPF: permit tcp any any eq 22 and permit ospf any any. Next create three class-maps: CM_SSH referencing the SSH ACL, CM_OSPF referencing the OSPF ACL, and CM_DEFAULT_CP matching default-class. Then create a policy-map PM_COPP that applies police statements: 8000 bps for SSH, 16000 bps for OSPF, and 4000 bps for the default class, choosing drop for exceed actions. Apply the policy in control-plane service-policy input PM_COPP. Finally configure control-plane host management-interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0 allow ssh snmp. Save your configuration when verified. If you implement this remotely, ensure you have a console session or an out-of-band path before applying MPP. This procedure gives you the exact commands to type and a clear rollback plan if you lose access. What is your first verification command after applying the service-policy? Lab: Implementing CoPP and MPP on R1 (Starter Commands) means follow acl → class-map → policy-map → control-plane service-policy, then set mpp management-interface entries and verify with show commands.. In practical terms, step-by-step starter configuration for the hands-on scenario. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Simulating an Attack and Observing CoPP Behavior
screens.subtitle: How to simulate a control-plane flood and confirm CoPP mitigates CPU impact

narration.text: A useful exercise is to simulate a control-plane flood from a test host and observe how CoPP handles the traffic. In the planning phase, ensure the test is done in a lab or on a maintenance segment, and keep out-of-band recovery ready. A common simulation uses a rapid ping or crafted traffic from a sender to the router’s control plane addresses. With CoPP applied, use show policy-map control-plane to watch the matched packets and drops increase for the default or targeted classes. If CoPP was configured correctly, drops will climb for the abusive class while packets for protected classes like SSH or OSPF remain within their CIR allowances. This demonstrates that policing is preventing C P U overload and preserving critical functions. A misconception to avoid is believing CoPP eliminates all impact; it mitigates by limiting rate, but excessive sustained attacks should also be handled with upstream filtering or scrubbing. After simulation, review counters, correlate router C P U and adjacency health, and adjust policing values if legitimate control traffic was adversely affected. What monitoring indicator would tell you CoPP preserved routing stability during the test?

keyIdea.title: Simulation lesson

Expected result
Abusive traffic should be dropped or policed while critical classes remain within their allowed rates, preserving adjacencies and management sessions.
Observability
Key places to watch: show policy-map control-plane counters, CPU utilization, and routing adjacency states. If adjacencies drop, policing is too strict for routing classes.
Mitigation beyond CoPP

screens.title: Common Mistakes and How to Avoid Them
screens.subtitle: Tuning pitfalls, lockout risks, and verification oversights

narration.text: Several recurring mistakes appear when teams first deploy CoPP and MPP. One is over-aggressive policing: choosing CIR or burst values too low for legitimate routing traffic. This causes OSPF or BGP adjacency failures during convergence. Another is overly broad ACLs for class-maps, which increase the chance of allowing abusive traffic or misclassifying flows. A third is applying MPP without ensuring an out-of-band path, which can lock administrators out of a remote device. To avoid these problems, follow a methodical approach: inventory control-plane flows and expected rates; scope ACLs to trusted source ranges; start with conservative policing values; apply policies in a lab; and always keep a console or out-of-band recovery method when changing MPP. Verification and monitoring are not optional — use show policy-map control-plane and cross-check against management system logs. The practical contrast to hold in mind is that CoPP defends the control plane by rate-limiting traffic types, while MPP restricts which interfaces management traffic may use; both must be coordinated to keep devices secure and accessible. What rollback step would you prepare before applying a restrictive MPP rule remotely?

keyIdea.title: Avoid pitfalls
keyIdea.text: Don’t choose policing values blindly, scope ACLs tightly, test in lab, and always keep a recovery path before changing MPP or CoPP in production.

Top mistakes
  • Setting CIR or BC too low for routing protocols.
  • Using overly broad ACLs for management traffic.
  • Applying MPP remotely without out-of-band console access.
  • Failing to monitor show policy-map control-plane after changes.
How to avoid them
Start conservative
Deploy low-impact policing in lab, then raise CIR/BC after observing legitimate traffic behavior.
Document and rollback
Write explicit rollback steps and maintain console access before applying MPP to production devices.
